---
title: "The Triangle of Everything"
subtitle: "Session 1 · Part C — rebuilding the chart of all objects in the Universe"
engine: markdown
pyodide:
  packages:
    - numpy
    - matplotlib
---

In 2023, two astrophysicists published a chart that went viral: **every
object in the Universe on one pair of axes** — quarks, viruses, fleas,
whales, planets, stars, black holes, galaxies, and the observable Universe
itself (Lineweaver & Patel, *All objects and some questions*, American
Journal of Physics 91:819). Plot mass against radius on log scales and
everything that exists falls inside a **triangle**: one wall drawn by
gravity, one wall drawn by quantum mechanics, and an apex where the two
meet at the smallest possible object.

In this part you rebuild that chart step by step. Every ingredient is
something you can compute: two axes, one curated table, one fact about
spheres, and two famous formulas. By the end you will have drawn the
figure — and you will know why it has the shape it has.

The rebuild happens in five steps:

| Step | What you add | What it teaches |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | axes + five familiar objects | log scales across ~100 decades |
| 2 | the full table, coloured by kind | curating and encoding a dataset |
| 3 | lines of constant density | why spheres make slope-3 lines |
| 4 | the black-hole and quantum walls | physical limits as plotted lines |
| 5 | the apex | where the walls meet: the Planck scale |

All code runs in your browser. The first cell may take a few seconds while
Python loads.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
import js
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pyodide.http import open_url

# Data files live beside this page; the Python worker runs from site_libs/.
DATA_URL = js.location.href.split("site_libs/")[0] + "data/"

plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.figsize": (9, 5),
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid": True,
    "grid.alpha": 0.22,
    "font.size": 11,
})

# Physical constants, cgs units (grams, centimetres, seconds)
G    = 6.674e-8       # gravitational constant [cm^3 g^-1 s^-2]
c    = 2.998e10       # speed of light [cm/s]
hbar = 1.055e-27      # reduced Planck constant [erg s]
H0   = 70 / 3.086e19  # Hubble constant: 70 km/s/Mpc, converted to [1/s]

print("Environment ready.")
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| include: false
# Pre-build every name the page uses, so each cell works no matter which
# cells were run before it. The visible cells re-derive all of this.
text = open_url(DATA_URL + "objects_universe.csv").read()
rows = [line.split(",") for line in text.strip().split("\n")[1:]]
names  = [r[0] for r in rows]
groups = [r[1] for r in rows]
mass   = np.array([float(r[2]) for r in rows])
radius = np.array([float(r[3]) for r in rows])

group_colours = {
    "particles":         "#666666",
    "life":              "#30a8b1",
    "worlds":            "#4269d0",
    "stars":             "#c98a00",
    "black holes":       "#171717",
    "cosmic structures": "#9475cd",
}

LABEL_LEFT  = {"Higgs boson", "white dwarf", "globular cluster"}
LABEL_BELOW = {"neutron star", "Ceres"}

def draw_objects(ax, fontsize=7.5):
    for i, nm in enumerate(names):
        col = group_colours[groups[i]]
        ax.scatter(radius[i], mass[i], s=18, color=col, zorder=3)
        if nm in LABEL_LEFT:
            ax.annotate(nm + " ", (radius[i], mass[i]), fontsize=fontsize,
                        color=col, zorder=3, ha="right")
        elif nm in LABEL_BELOW:
            ax.annotate(" " + nm, (radius[i], mass[i]), fontsize=fontsize,
                        color=col, zorder=3, va="top")
        else:
            ax.annotate(" " + nm, (radius[i], mass[i]), fontsize=fontsize,
                        color=col, zorder=3)

def cosmos_axes(figsize=(10, 10)):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_xlim(1e-35, 1e30); ax.set_ylim(1e-40, 1e60)
    ax.set_xticks([10.0**k for k in range(-35, 31, 5)])
    ax.set_yticks([10.0**k for k in range(-40, 61, 10)])
    ax.set_xlabel("radius (cm)"); ax.set_ylabel("mass (g)")
    return fig, ax

r_line = np.logspace(-35, 30, 200)

def mass_at_density(rho, r):
    return 4/3 * np.pi * rho * r**3

def schwarzschild_mass(r):
    return r * c**2 / (2 * G)

def compton_mass(r):
    return hbar / (r * c)

rho_all = mass / (4/3 * np.pi * radius**3)
l_p = np.sqrt(hbar * G / c**3)
m_p = np.sqrt(hbar * c / G)
r_x = np.sqrt(2 * G * hbar / c**3)
m_x = np.sqrt(hbar * c / (2 * G))
rho_human = rho_all[names.index("human")]
iU = names.index("observable Universe")
ratio = 2 * G * mass[iU] / c**2 / radius[iU]
```

## 1 · One pair of axes for everything

Why mass and radius? Because they are the two properties **every physical
object has**. A virus has no temperature you can easily assign, a galaxy
has no chemistry — but both have a mass and a size. If you want a chart of
*everything*, you need axes everything can land on.

The catch is range. From a neutrino to the observable Universe, mass spans
about **90 orders of magnitude** and radius about **44**. On linear axes,
one pixel that shows the Universe would hide the entire Sun inside a
region a trillion-trillion times smaller than the pixel. So both axes are
logarithmic — the same move you made for allometry in Part A, stretched to
its absolute limit. (We work in grams and centimetres, following the
paper; on axes this wide the choice of unit just slides everything by a
constant, and changes nothing about the shape.)

The chart's raw material is a curated table — one row per object, a name,
a group, a mass and a radius:

```{pyodide}
text = open_url(DATA_URL + "objects_universe.csv").read()
rows = [line.split(",") for line in text.strip().split("\n")[1:]]
names  = [r[0] for r in rows]
groups = [r[1] for r in rows]
mass   = np.array([float(r[2]) for r in rows])
radius = np.array([float(r[3]) for r in rows])

for r in rows[:6]:
    print(f"{r[0]:<14} {r[1]:<12} {float(r[2]):>10.2e} g {float(r[3]):>10.2e} cm")
print(f"... {len(names)} objects in total")
```

```{pyodide}
assert len(names) == 29
assert mass.max() / mass.min() > 1e89
assert radius.max() / radius.min() > 1e43
print("✓ 29 objects; mass spans 90 orders of magnitude, radius spans 44")
```

Start with five things you have an intuition for:

```{pyodide}
FAMILIAR = ["flea", "human", "blue whale", "Earth", "Sun"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5.5))
for nm in FAMILIAR:
    i = names.index(nm)
    ax.scatter(radius[i], mass[i], s=30, color="#4269d0", zorder=3)
    ax.annotate(" " + nm, (radius[i], mass[i]), fontsize=10)
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("radius (cm)"); ax.set_ylabel("mass (g)")
ax.set_title("Five familiar objects — already 29 orders of magnitude in mass")
plt.show()
```

Notice they fall roughly on a straight line. Hold that thought — it is the
key to Step 3.

First, a confession about the data. What is "the radius of a human"? The
paper treats you as a **sphere of radius 50 cm** with mass 70 kg. Check
what that implies:

```{pyodide}
i = names.index("human")
rho_human = mass[i] / (4/3 * np.pi * radius[i]**3)
print(f"implied human density: {rho_human:.2f} g/cm³")
```

```{pyodide}
assert 0.1 < rho_human < 0.2
print("✓ the spherical human is ~0.13 g/cm³ — seven times fluffier than water")
```

Real humans are almost exactly water density; the 50-cm sphere
overestimates your volume about sevenfold. On an ordinary chart that would
be a scandal. Here, one decade of error is **one percent of the axis** —
invisible. That is the quiet trade this figure makes everywhere: every
value is an order-of-magnitude sketch, and at this scale that is exactly
good enough. Say so in the caption, and it is honest; hide it, and it
is not.

## 2 · The full bestiary

Now all 29 objects, coloured by kind. Six groups: particles (grey), life,
worlds, stars, black holes (black, naturally), and cosmic structures. The
palette is colour-blind-checked, and every point carries its own label —
colour alone is never the only way to tell things apart:

```{pyodide}
group_colours = {
    "particles":         "#666666",
    "life":              "#30a8b1",
    "worlds":            "#4269d0",
    "stars":             "#c98a00",
    "black holes":       "#171717",
    "cosmic structures": "#9475cd",
}

LABEL_LEFT  = {"Higgs boson", "white dwarf", "globular cluster"}
LABEL_BELOW = {"neutron star", "Ceres"}

def draw_objects(ax, fontsize=7.5):
    for i, nm in enumerate(names):
        col = group_colours[groups[i]]
        ax.scatter(radius[i], mass[i], s=18, color=col, zorder=3)
        if nm in LABEL_LEFT:      # nudge a few labels out of collisions
            ax.annotate(nm + " ", (radius[i], mass[i]), fontsize=fontsize,
                        color=col, zorder=3, ha="right")
        elif nm in LABEL_BELOW:
            ax.annotate(" " + nm, (radius[i], mass[i]), fontsize=fontsize,
                        color=col, zorder=3, va="top")
        else:
            ax.annotate(" " + nm, (radius[i], mass[i]), fontsize=fontsize,
                        color=col, zorder=3)

def cosmos_axes(figsize=(10, 10)):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_xlim(1e-35, 1e30); ax.set_ylim(1e-40, 1e60)
    ax.set_xticks([10.0**k for k in range(-35, 31, 5)])
    ax.set_yticks([10.0**k for k in range(-40, 61, 10)])
    ax.set_xlabel("radius (cm)"); ax.set_ylabel("mass (g)")
    return fig, ax

fig, ax = cosmos_axes()
draw_objects(ax)
ax.set_title("All 29 objects — note the two great empty corners")
plt.show()
```

The interesting thing is not where the points are — it is where they
**aren't**. Nothing in the top-left (small but monstrously heavy), nothing
in the bottom-right (huge but almost massless). Two whole corners of
possibility, empty. The rest of this page explains why they *must* be.

## 3 · Density is a straight line here

Any object of roughly uniform density $\rho$ obeys
$m = \frac{4}{3}\pi \rho\, r^3$. Take logs and this becomes
$\log m = 3\log r + \text{const}$ — on our axes, **a straight line of
slope 3**, one line per density. Chemistry pins atomic matter near
$\rho \approx 1\ \text{g/cm}^3$; nuclear matter sits fourteen decades
higher:

```{pyodide}
r_line = np.logspace(-35, 30, 200)

def mass_at_density(rho, r):
    return 4/3 * np.pi * rho * r**3

fig, ax = cosmos_axes()
draw_objects(ax)
for rho in (1.0, 2.3e14):
    ax.plot(r_line, mass_at_density(rho, r_line), ls="--", lw=1, color="#888888")
ax.text(2e14, mass_at_density(1, 1e14), "atomic density", rotation=64,
        fontsize=9, color="#888888")
ax.text(2e2, mass_at_density(2.3e14, 1e2), "nuclear density", rotation=64,
        fontsize=9, color="#888888")
ax.set_title("Two densities organise almost everything")
plt.show()
```

Suddenly the scatter has a skeleton. Everything made of atoms — viruses,
fleas, whales, asteroids, planets, the Sun — strings out along the atomic
line: that *was* the straight line hiding in the five familiar objects.
The proton and the neutron star, fourteen decades apart in size, share the
nuclear line: **a neutron star really is matter at the density of an
atomic nucleus, the size of a city**.

```{pyodide}
rho_all = mass / (4/3 * np.pi * radius**3)

i_ns, i_p = names.index("neutron star"), names.index("proton")
assert 1e14 < rho_all[i_ns] < 1e15 and 1e14 < rho_all[i_p] < 1e15
assert rho_all[names.index("red giant")] < 1e-5
print("✓ proton and neutron star both sit at nuclear density, ~10¹⁴ g/cm³")
print(f"densest object:  {names[int(np.argmax(rho_all))]}")
print(f"fluffiest object: {names[int(np.argmin(rho_all))]}")
```

Read that last line again: the least dense thing in the Universe **is the
Universe** — about $10^{-29}\ \text{g/cm}^3$, six protons per cubic metre.

### Your turn: interrogate the densities {#sec-ex-density}

You have `rho_all` for all 29 objects. Rank everything by density and
print a table from densest to fluffiest, with the group and the density of
each object. Then answer from your output: which **group** owns the top of
the table, and how many decades of density separate a red giant from a
white dwarf — two objects of nearly the same *mass*?

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_density

names  = [r[0] for r in rows]
groups = [r[1] for r in rows]
mass   = np.array([float(r[2]) for r in rows])
radius = np.array([float(r[3]) for r in rows])
rho_all = mass / (4/3 * np.pi * radius**3)
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_density
# `names`, `groups`, `mass`, `radius` and `rho_all` are all loaded.
# 1. Get the object order sorted by density, densest first.
# 2. Print rank, name, group, density for every object.
# 3. Compute the red giant / white dwarf density gap in decades.

order = ______

for rank, i in enumerate(order, 1):
    print(f"{rank:>2}. {names[i]:<20} {groups[i]:<18} {rho_all[i]:>9.1e} g/cm³")

gap = ______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_density"}
**Hint 1** — `np.argsort(rho_all)` gives indices from *smallest* to
largest; reverse it with `[::-1]` to get densest first.
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_density"}
**Hint 2** — A "decade" is a factor of ten, so the gap in decades is
`np.log10(rho_wd / rho_rg)`. Get each with
`rho_all[names.index("white dwarf")]`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_density"}
**Fully worked solution:**

```python
order = np.argsort(rho_all)[::-1]

for rank, i in enumerate(order, 1):
    print(f"{rank:>2}. {names[i]:<20} {groups[i]:<18} {rho_all[i]:>9.1e} g/cm³")

gap = np.log10(rho_all[names.index("white dwarf")]
               / rho_all[names.index("red giant")])
print(f"\nred giant vs white dwarf: {gap:.0f} decades of density")
```

The top of the table belongs entirely to **particles** — the top quark
and Higgs boson are the densest "objects" plotted, though for them
density is a strange notion (their radius is a quantum limit, not a
surface). The red giant and white dwarf differ by roughly **12 decades**
of density despite nearly identical masses — they are the same kind of
star at two different moments of its life, which is why mass alone tells
you so little and the mass–radius *pair* tells you so much.
:::

## 4 · The two walls

Now the physics that gives the chart its shape. Both walls are one-line
formulas.

**The gravity wall.** Squeeze a mass $m$ into a small enough radius and
it becomes a black hole. That radius is the Schwarzschild radius
$r_s = 2Gm/c^2$ — for a given radius, the heaviest possible object is
$m = rc^2/2G$: **slope +1** on our axes. Nothing can sit above this line:
an object of that mass would already have collapsed. Black holes sit
exactly *on* it — that is what a black hole is.

**The quantum wall.** Quantum mechanics denies small masses a definite
tiny size: a particle of mass $m$ cannot be localised below its Compton
wavelength $\lambda_c = \hbar / mc$, so the lightest possible object of
radius $r$ is $m = \hbar/rc$: **slope −1**. Below this line, "object"
stops meaning anything — try to confine a particle tighter and you create
new particles instead. Fundamental particles (top quark, Higgs, electron,
neutrino) are plotted *on* their Compton wavelengths; the composite proton
gets its measured charge radius.

```{pyodide}
def schwarzschild_mass(r):   # heaviest object of radius r (it's a black hole)
    return r * c**2 / (2 * G)

def compton_mass(r):         # lightest object of radius r (quantum limit)
    return hbar / (r * c)

fig, ax = cosmos_axes()
ax.fill_between(r_line, schwarzschild_mass(r_line), 1e60,
                color="#e66852", alpha=0.15, zorder=0)
ax.fill_between(r_line, 1e-40, compton_mass(r_line),
                color="#4269d0", alpha=0.15, zorder=0)
ax.plot(r_line, schwarzschild_mass(r_line), color="#171717", lw=1.4)
ax.plot(r_line, compton_mass(r_line), color="#171717", lw=1.4)
draw_objects(ax)
ax.text(3e-14, 1e45, "forbidden by gravity", rotation=38, fontsize=13, color="#8a3324")
ax.text(3e-5, 1e-24, "quantum uncertainty", rotation=-38, fontsize=13, color="#1d3f8f")
ax.set_title("The two walls: nothing above the black-hole line, nothing below Compton")
plt.show()
```

The empty corners of Step 2 are now explained — and shaded. They are not
unexplored; they are **impossible**. This is the deepest trick in the
figure: the *absence* of data is carrying the physics, and the shading
turns absence into a statement.

One object deserves a second look. Check the top-right corner:

```{pyodide}
iU = names.index("observable Universe")
ratio = 2 * G * mass[iU] / c**2 / radius[iU]
print(f"Universe: Schwarzschild radius / actual radius = {ratio:.2f}")
```

```{pyodide}
assert 0.8 < ratio < 1.2
print("✓ the observable Universe sits ON the black-hole line")
```

The Universe's mass and radius satisfy the black-hole relation almost
exactly. Does that mean we live inside a black hole? The paper's answer
is careful: the Schwarzschild formula assumes empty space *outside* the
object, and outside our Hubble volume the density carries on much the
same — so no. But *why* the numbers land on the line so precisely is the
second exercise.

## 5 · The apex, and the finished chart

Walls of slope +1 and −1 must meet. Set them equal:

$$\frac{rc^2}{2G} = \frac{\hbar}{rc}
\;\;\Rightarrow\;\;
r = \sqrt{\frac{2G\hbar}{c^3}},\qquad
m = \sqrt{\frac{\hbar c}{2G}}.$$

```{pyodide}
r_x = np.sqrt(2 * G * hbar / c**3)
m_x = np.sqrt(hbar * c / (2 * G))
l_p = np.sqrt(hbar * G / c**3)    # Planck length
m_p = np.sqrt(hbar * c / G)       # Planck mass

print(f"walls cross at    r = {r_x:.2e} cm,  m = {m_x:.2e} g")
print(f"Planck scale:   l_p = {l_p:.2e} cm, m_p = {m_p:.2e} g")
```

```{pyodide}
assert abs(r_x / (np.sqrt(2) * l_p) - 1) < 1e-6
assert abs(m_x / (m_p / np.sqrt(2)) - 1) < 1e-6
print("✓ the walls cross at the Planck scale (times a factor of √2)")
```

The crossing point is the **Planck scale** — about $10^{-33}$ cm and
$2\times10^{-5}$ g, the mass of a flea's egg compressed to a point
$10^{20}$ times smaller than a proton. The smallest possible object is a
Planck-mass black hole, which the paper calls an **instanton**: the only
thing that is simultaneously as small as gravity allows and as small as
quantum mechanics allows. Left of the Planck length, physics has no
tested theory at all — the paper shades it "sub-Planckian unknown", and
so will we.

Now assemble everything — regions, walls, density skeleton, objects,
apex:

```{pyodide}
fig, ax = cosmos_axes(figsize=(10.5, 10.5))

# forbidden regions
ax.fill_between(r_line, schwarzschild_mass(r_line), 1e60,
                color="#e66852", alpha=0.15, zorder=0)
ax.fill_between(r_line, 1e-40, compton_mass(r_line),
                color="#4269d0", alpha=0.15, zorder=0)
ax.axvspan(1e-35, l_p, color="#555555", alpha=0.25, zorder=0)

# the two walls
ax.plot(r_line, schwarzschild_mass(r_line), color="#171717", lw=1.4)
ax.plot(r_line, compton_mass(r_line), color="#171717", lw=1.4)

# density skeleton
for rho in (1.0, 2.3e14):
    ax.plot(r_line, mass_at_density(rho, r_line), ls="--", lw=0.9,
            color="#999999", zorder=1)

# every object, plus the apex
draw_objects(ax)
ax.scatter([l_p], [m_p], marker="D", s=45, color="#171717", zorder=4)
ax.annotate("  instanton\n  (Planck scale)", (l_p, m_p), fontsize=8.5)

# annotations
ax.text(3e-14, 1e45, "forbidden by gravity", rotation=38, fontsize=13, color="#8a3324")
ax.text(3e-5, 1e-24, "quantum uncertainty", rotation=-38, fontsize=13, color="#1d3f8f")
ax.text(1.7e-35, 1e10, "sub-Planckian unknown", rotation=90, fontsize=9, color="#444444")
ax.text(1e-24, 3e6, "black holes", rotation=38, fontsize=9, color="#171717")
ax.text(2.5e-10, 3e-21, "Compton limit", rotation=-38, fontsize=9, color="#171717")
ax.text(2e14, mass_at_density(1, 1e14), "atomic density", rotation=64,
        fontsize=9, color="#888888")
ax.text(2e2, mass_at_density(2.3e14, 1e2), "nuclear density", rotation=64,
        fontsize=9, color="#888888")
ax.set_title("Everything in the Universe, one chart — after Lineweaver & Patel (2023)")
plt.show()
```

That is the triangle of everything: gravity above, quantum uncertainty
below, the unknown to the left, the Universe pinned to the top of the
gravity wall, and every known thing strung out on density lines in
between.

### Your turn: put the Universe on the wall {#sec-ex-hubble}

The Universe's point was given to you in the table. Derive it. All you
need is the Hubble constant. The radius of the observable Universe is the
Hubble radius $r_H = c/H_0$; its average density is the critical density
$\rho_c = 3H_0^2 / 8\pi G$; and its mass is that density times the volume
of the Hubble sphere. Then test whether your derived Universe lands on
the black-hole line.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_hubble
import numpy as np
G    = 6.674e-8       # [cm^3 g^-1 s^-2]
c    = 2.998e10       # [cm/s]
H0   = 70 / 3.086e19  # [1/s]
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_hubble
# Constants G, c and H0 are loaded (cgs units).
# 1. Hubble radius, critical density, and the mass of the Hubble sphere.
# 2. Schwarzschild radius of that mass — how does it compare to r_H?

r_H   = ______
rho_c = ______
m_U   = ______

r_s = 2 * G * m_U / c**2
print(f"r_H = {r_H:.2e} cm   m_U = {m_U:.2e} g")
print(f"Schwarzschild radius of the Universe's mass: {r_s:.2e} cm")
print(f"ratio r_s / r_H = {r_s / r_H:.3f}")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_hubble"}
**Hint 1** — `r_H = c / H0`, `rho_c = 3 * H0**2 / (8 * np.pi * G)`, and
the mass is density × volume of a sphere of radius `r_H`.
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_hubble"}
**Hint 2** — `m_U = 4/3 * np.pi * r_H**3 * rho_c`. If your ratio is not
extremely close to 1, check your powers and parentheses.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_hubble"}
**Fully worked solution:**

```python
r_H   = c / H0
rho_c = 3 * H0**2 / (8 * np.pi * G)
m_U   = 4/3 * np.pi * r_H**3 * rho_c

r_s = 2 * G * m_U / c**2
print(f"r_H = {r_H:.2e} cm   m_U = {m_U:.2e} g")
print(f"Schwarzschild radius of the Universe's mass: {r_s:.2e} cm")
print(f"ratio r_s / r_H = {r_s / r_H:.3f}")
```

The ratio is **exactly 1** — and not by coincidence. Substitute the
formulas into each other:

$$r_s = \frac{2G}{c^2}\cdot\frac{4}{3}\pi r_H^3 \cdot \frac{3H_0^2}{8\pi G}
     = \frac{r_H^3 H_0^2}{c^2}
     = r_H \left(\frac{r_H H_0}{c}\right)^2 = r_H.$$

Every constant cancels. A Universe at critical density *must* sit on the
black-hole line, whatever the value of $H_0$ — the "coincidence" in the
chart is algebra wearing a costume. This is a lesson about reading
charts, not just making them: when a data point lands suspiciously
exactly on a theory line, check whether the two were secretly computed
from the same ingredients.
:::

## What went into the chart

Count the ingredients you actually used:

- **one curated table** — 29 rows, every value an order-of-magnitude
  sketch, sources mixed from measurement (Earth), convention (the 50-cm
  spherical human), and definition (black-hole radii);
- **two log axes** — doing more work than everything else combined,
  turning 90 orders of magnitude into a readable square and power laws
  into straight lines;
- **one fact about spheres** — $m \propto \rho r^3$, which organises all
  atomic matter onto one line and all nuclear matter onto another;
- **two formulas** — $r_s = 2Gm/c^2$ and $\lambda_c = \hbar/mc$, drawn
  not as data but as *walls*, turning empty space into a claim;
- **annotation** — region labels, line labels, direct point labels: the
  difference between a scatter plot and an explanation.

That is the whole machine. The famous figure is not famous for its data —
half its rows you could have written down yourself — but for its
*framing*: pick axes everything shares, let physics draw the boundaries,
and the emptiness becomes the story.

## Sources and serving notes

- Lineweaver, C. H. & Patel, V. M. (2023) *All objects and some
  questions*, American Journal of Physics 91:819–825
  ([doi:10.1119/5.0150209](https://doi.org/10.1119/5.0150209)) — the
  original Figure 2, which this page rebuilds in simplified form (we omit
  the cosmological-epoch background shading and plot a smaller object
  sample).
- `objects_universe.csv` is curated for this course: masses and radii are
  order-of-magnitude values assembled from standard references; the
  human and whale entries deliberately reproduce the paper's values,
  sphericity and all. Fundamental particles are plotted at their Compton
  wavelengths (the proton at its measured charge radius); black holes at
  their Schwarzschild radii.
- Constants: CODATA values rounded to 4 significant figures;
  $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc.
